analysis.one_liner: Requires credit bureaus to get your written permission before sharing your credit report.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by a single senator with no cosponsors, the bill received one Senate Banking Committee hearing in July 2018 and died without a vote when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, credit bureaus can share your credit report with lenders, insurers, and marketers unless you take action to stop it. This bill flips that default: bureaus could only share your report for credit or insurance purposes if you gave written consent first. It would also ban bureaus from charging you fees for controlling your own file, require them to take reasonable steps to prevent data breaches, and order a government study on how to better protect the data they collect.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers. Anyone whose credit file is bought and sold by the three major credit bureaus would gain control over who sees it. People affected by data breaches would benefit from required security practices, and consumers would no longer pay fees to lock or access their own credit reports.

how_it_helps.text: Flips the default from opt-out to opt-in: a credit bureau could share your report for a new credit or insurance transaction only after you give affirmative written consent with proper identification.
Bans consumer reporting agencies from charging consumers any fee for activities under the consent rules, so controlling access to your own file would be free.
Requires bureaus to use commercially reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized access to consumer reports, including complying with data-security standards under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act.

Requires the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to set up a secure, convenient, and cost-free method for consumers to allow or block sharing of their reports, with changes taking effect within two business days.
Directs the Government Accountability Office to study what additional protections are needed to keep information in consumer files secure, with specific legislative recommendations due within a year.
Requires bureaus to disclose to consumers all information they hold about them, including information held by parent companies, subsidiaries, or affiliates, upon written request.

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting agencies, whose business of selling consumer reports and marketing lists would require consumer consent, and lenders and insurers that rely on prescreened reports and unsolicited offers of credit and insurance to reach customers.

drawbacks.text: Requiring written consent before every credit or insurance report pull could add friction and delay to routine transactions like applying for a loan, a credit card, or insurance, which lenders would argue raises costs.

Because unsolicited offers of credit and insurance would also require opt-in consent, consumers who never opt in would stop receiving prescreened offers, some of which are competitively priced deals they might have wanted.

The security provision requires only 'commercially reasonable efforts' to prevent breaches rather than a hard standard with penalties, and much of the bill's oversight value depends on future CFPB rulemaking and a GAO study rather than immediate protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — consumers deciding who sees their financial data, at no cost to themselves — is real and directly responsive to the risk that bureaus profit from selling data consumers cannot easily control. The costs are modest friction in credit and insurance applications and the loss of unsolicited offers some consumers value. The bill's weakest point is enforcement: 'commercially reasonable efforts' on security is a soft standard, and its biggest items are studies and rulemaking rather than immediate rules.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee took the bill in, held one hearing, and never voted on it, so it expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the bill on January 30, 2018, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The Banking Committee held a hearing on July 12, 2018 (printed as S.Hrg. 115-361), but the bill never received a committee vote or floor action.
The bill died at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019, without ever reaching a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and the lenders and insurers that buy their data are better off, because the opt-out default stays in place and they can continue using and selling consumer credit files without asking permission. Consumers gained nothing beyond the free security-freeze rights adopted separately that year.

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over credit reporting law
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill and held one hearing on July 12, 2018, but never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a committee vote during the two years it sat in the panel.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure; the bill had one Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and died in a Republican-led committee without a markup.

industries.note: Their core business — compiling and selling consumer credit reports and marketing lists — would require the consumer's written consent first, and they could no longer charge consumers fees for accessing or controlling their own files. Consumers' interest in controlling their data runs directly against the bureaus' interest in selling it freely.

industries.industry: Lenders and insurers that prescreen customers
industries.note: Firm offers of credit and insurance could still be made, but only to consumers who opted in, shrinking the prescreened marketing lists these companies use to find customers without consumers asking. Their gain from unsolicited access to consumer files is the consumers' loss of privacy.
